profiles.meeting_scenario: A troubleshooting meeting at a public-interest land law clinic in Nairobi that is revising a comparative guidance note for a regional municipal forum on housing land delivery in Enugu, Kampala, Maseru, Gaborone, and Eldoret. After circulation of the draft, partner city legal officers and planning officials said the note was insightful but difficult to use when handling recurring problems around ownership disputes, subdivision, and dealings with non-state land actors. The meeting is meant to diagnose why the draft is not functioning as an operational troubleshooting tool across the five cities and to decide how to revise it before recirculation. The agenda is to identify the real source of the draft's failure, determine which examples and cautions should anchor the revision, and agree on a concrete repair strategy. The expected outcome is agreement on how to make the guidance more actionable, which conflict material should frame the revisions, and what form the city-specific additions should take.

members.name: Amina Njoroge
members.expertise: Comparative land law, municipal advisory work, statutory compliance, and legal framing of hybrid land administration practices
members.background: Amina is a Kenyan lawyer who has advised county governments, urban reform projects, and municipal legal departments across East and Southern Africa, often translating socio-legal research into guidance that city lawyers can stand behind.
members.private_state: She wants the revised note to remain analytically credible while being safe for municipal legal officers to rely on, and she is especially worried that the clinic could appear to normalize extra-statutory land practices if the wording is too open-ended.
hidden_assumptions: If guidance is described as 'actionable,' it must be framed so a city legal or planning office can act on it without exceeding recognized authority.
The most probative 'conflict cases' are the disputes that became formal files, enforcement actions, administrative reviews, or court matters because those create legally reviewable fact patterns.
To 'strengthen the memo' means making the propositions more defensible by tightening legal characterization and evidentiary anchoring rather than broadening the narrative.
When colleagues suggest adding 'city-specific notes,' the natural form is short jurisdictional qualifiers attached to recommendations, not free-standing illustrations.
Examples from different cities can be compared safely only after they are translated into common categories of authority, procedure, and compliance.

members.name: David Okello
members.role: Field Research Lead on Urban Land Delivery
members.expertise: Socio-legal fieldwork, informal and customary land transactions, dispute pathways, and comparative institutional analysis in African cities
members.background: David is a Ugandan researcher trained in urban studies and law who coordinated interviews and case tracing with chiefs, brokers, planning officers, local allocators, and residents in Kampala and Eldoret and contributed to synthesis across all five cities.
members.private_state: He wants to preserve the note's central claim that cooperation between state and non-state actors often keeps land delivery functioning, and he worries that excessive legal narrowing will strip out the mechanisms that actually explain compliance, conflict, and accommodation.
hidden_assumptions: If guidance is described as 'actionable,' it should help officials and practitioners intervene in the transactions and disputes that actually occur on the ground, even where formal law only partly captures them.

The most revealing 'conflict cases' include recurrent disputes that are settled through local mediation, broker networks, chiefs, or administrative improvisation before they ever enter a formal record.
To 'strengthen the memo' means making the analysis more persuasive by grounding claims in thicker institutional explanation and clearer cross-city examples.
When colleagues propose 'city-specific notes,' the obvious form is brief practice vignettes showing how accommodation already works in each city.
Comparability across the five cities depends on preserving the social process around land delivery, not only the formal legal categories into which those processes can be translated.

misalignment_points.topic: What it means to make the guidance actionable
misalignment_points.surface_form: Both agree the revised note needs to be 'more actionable' for city users.
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: M1 believes 'more actionable' means recommendations are framed tightly enough that municipal legal and planning officers can rely on them without seeming to authorize conduct outside formal statutory powers.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: M2 believes 'more actionable' means the note should help officials respond to the real transaction chains, dispute habits, and negotiated accommodations through which land is actually delivered.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: Actionability is a routine praise term in policy-law meetings, and both members sincerely want the note to be more useful to cities, so each treats their own criterion as the obvious practical meaning.

misalignment_points.topic: Which disputes count as the conflict cases
misalignment_points.surface_form: Both refer to revising the note around 'the conflict cases' on ownership and subdivision.
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: M1 means the subset of disputes that generated formal municipal files, planning enforcement, land board review, or litigation in cities such as Maseru, Gaborone, and Eldoret.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: M2 means the broader recurring disputes documented in fieldwork, including broker-mediated double sales, chief-validated allocations, boundary friction, and informal subdivision disagreements that were often settled locally in Kampala or Enugu before formal filing.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: In land governance work, 'conflict cases' sounds like neutral shorthand for the relevant dispute evidence, and both assume the other is naturally referring to the same body of examples without needing to specify whether it is file-based or field-observed.

misalignment_points.topic: What it means to strengthen the memo
misalignment_points.surface_form: Both agree they need to 'strengthen the memo' before sending the revision back out.
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: M1 assumes this means sharpening the memo's claims by refining the recommendations, clarifying where accommodation is merely tolerated rather than legally grounded, and tightening the framing around authority and compliance.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: M2 assumes this means strengthening the memo's explanatory force by adding more concrete institutional detail in the city analysis so the recommendations are visibly grounded in how cooperation and non-compliance actually work.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: The phrase 'strengthen the memo' comfortably covers both rigor and grounding, so the surface agreement feels natural and competent; neither hears the phrase as requiring a discussion about whether the revision is mainly a legal tightening exercise or a broader analytical reinforcement.

misalignment_points.topic: What form city-specific notes should take
misalignment_points.surface_form: Both agree to add 'city-specific notes' to avoid overgeneralizing across the five cities.
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: M1 assumes these notes will be short jurisdiction-specific qualifiers placed under each recommendation, flagging formal limits on reliance on chiefs, brokers, plot allocators, or administrative workarounds in each city.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: M2 assumes these notes will be short city vignettes attached to the analytical sections, showing concrete pathways of mutual accommodation in places like Kampala, Enugu, or Gaborone.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: The phrase 'city-specific notes' sounds like a minor editorial add-on rather than a substantive design choice, and each member takes their preferred format to be the standard way such notes would naturally be inserted.

turns.inner_thought: The draft is good, but the partner officers are telling us they cannot safely pick it up and use it. If we say the revision should be more actionable, that has to mean a municipal legal or planning office can rely on it without looking as though we are inviting action outside recognized authority. I need to move us toward tighter propositions and firmer guardrails.
turns.utterance: Thanks for joining. My sense is the draft is analytically strong, but it still is not actionable enough for the city officers who are meant to use it when these recurring land delivery problems come up.

turns.inner_thought: I agree with that, but for me the gap is that the note still does not help officials step into the transaction chains and dispute habits that actually shape land delivery. If it is going to be more actionable, it has to speak to the institutions people already use, not just the narrow formal record.
turns.utterance: I think that's right. It needs to be more actionable, and at the moment it still doesn't show clearly enough how city users can work through the institutions people already rely on.

turns.inner_thought: We should reorganize around the conflict cases that produced formal files, reviews, enforcement, or litigation. Those are the strongest materials because they reveal where accommodation collided with authority in a way the city can actually stand over.
turns.utterance: If we're repairing it, I'd anchor the revision around the strongest conflict cases on ownership and subdivision. That's where the current note is closest to something city users can work from.

turns.inner_thought: Yes, the conflict cases are the recurring disputes we traced across the fieldwork, including the ones settled before they ever became files. The repeated patterns—double sales, boundary friction, subdivision fights—are what make the analysis useful across cities.
turns.utterance: I agree on using the conflict cases. Once you line them up, you can see the same ownership and subdivision problems returning across Kampala, Enugu, and Eldoret in a way that should help the revision.

turns.inner_thought: What we really need is to strengthen the memo by tightening the recommendations and sharpening the legal characterization. The note currently slides too easily between what cities observe and what they can properly rely on.
turns.utterance: For me, the main task now is to strengthen the memo before it goes back out. At the moment some of the propositions are doing too much work at once.

turns.inner_thought: Yes, strengthen the memo—but by making the analysis more persuasive and visibly grounded in how cooperation, compliance, and accommodation actually differ across the five cities. Otherwise the recommendations will still feel abstract to users.
turns.utterance: Yes, we do need to strengthen the memo. I think part of that is making the city analysis do a bit more of the explanatory work for the reader.

turns.inner_thought: We should add city-specific notes as short qualifiers attached to each recommendation, so a municipal reader can see where reliance has limits in Maseru versus Kampala or Eldoret. That is the safest way to avoid overgeneralizing.
turns.utterance: A practical way to handle that would be to add city-specific notes, so we're not speaking across all five places as if the same caveats travel unchanged.

turns.inner_thought: Good—city-specific notes can carry brief vignettes from each city showing how accommodation already works around bottlenecks. That will preserve the social process instead of flattening everything into generic statements.
turns.utterance: I think city-specific notes would help a lot. They'd give us room to show the reader how the picture shifts from one city to another without overloading the main text.

turns.inner_thought: One reason the draft is not landing is that it sometimes treats observed success on the ground as if that alone is enough. It is not. City users need guidance they can formally stand behind, and we must not sound as though we are normalizing extra-statutory practice.
turns.utterance: I also think part of the trouble is that the draft occasionally assumes that because something is working, the user will know what to do with it. That's where it loses people.

turns.inner_thought: And from my side, it loses people where it names non-compliance but leaves out the routine accommodations that stop disputes from escalating. If we don't explain those, the note won't help with the actual problems officials face before matters harden into formal disputes.
turns.utterance: I see that. I also think there are places where the note stops one step too early and doesn't explain enough about how these situations are being managed in practice.

turns.inner_thought: We need a defensible starting point, so I want to begin with the cleaner documented dispute material from Maseru and Gaborone, where the authority questions are easier to characterize, and then refine the recommendations from there.
turns.utterance: In terms of sequence, I'd be inclined to start with the cleaner conflict cases from Maseru and Gaborone and use those to steady the revision before we widen back out.

turns.inner_thought: That's workable as long as I can still draw across all five cities. I'll gather the broader conflict cases, including the recurring locally managed disputes, and draft the city-specific notes as short city vignettes so the guidance stays grounded in actual pathways as well as the formal picture.
turns.utterance: That makes sense. I can take a first pass across all five cities, pull together the conflict cases, and draft the city-specific notes so the revised guidance stays grounded and is more actionable when we recirculate it.
